title: Closures with Mutable State: Bank Accounts and Memoized Fibonacci
description: Compare two closure patterns in Python: message-passing bank accounts with independent nonlocal balances and a memoization cache that cuts recursive Fibonacci calls.

steps.description: `make_account(balance)` defines three inner functions (`withdraw`, `deposit`, and `dispatch`) that share the enclosing `balance` parameter, and returns `dispatch`. Both `withdraw` (line 8) and `deposit` (line 15) declare `nonlocal balance` so their assignments mutate the captured `balance` rather than creating a new local variable.

Lines 31-32 create two independent closures `acc = make_account(100)` and `acc2 = make_account(100)`. Calling `acc("deposit")(50)` and `acc("withdraw")(30)` updates `acc`'s frame to `120`, while `acc2("balance")` stays `100` in its own frame.

`counted(name, f)` wraps `f` in a closure that increments `calls[name]` on every call (line 45). `memoize(f)` captures a private `cache = dict()` on line 50 and only calls `f(x)` on line 53 when `x not in cache`.
Look at `memoize`: `cache` is allocated once when `memoize(f)` is called on line 50, and every subsequent call to `wrapped(x)` looks up `x` in that same dictionary before computing `f(x)`.
Lines 57-69 wire up `slow = counted("slow", fib_slow)` without memoization and `fast = memoize(counted("fast", fib_fast))` with memoization, then lines 72-73 run both on `25`.

steps.question: When `fast(25)` runs on line 73, `memoize` sits outside `counted("fast", fib_fast)`. How many times does `cache` miss and call the underlying `counted` function for inputs `0` through `25`?
steps.answer: Each integer from `0` to `25` is computed once on its first cache miss and reused from `cache` thereafter, so `calls["fast"]` is `26` (compared to `242785` calls for `slow(25)`).

steps.description: At trace step 26 inside `acc("withdraw")(30)`, `withdraw` subtracts `30` from `acc`'s captured `balance` (`150`) on line 10, updating it to `120` while `acc2`'s `balance` remains `100`.
